description: General information about menopause - what it is, when it happens, and its impact

entries.title: What is Menopause?
entries.description: Definition and basic understanding of menopause
entries.content: Menopause is a natural biological process marking the end of a woman's reproductive years. It's defined as the point when you've gone 12 consecutive months without a menstrual period. Menopause occurs when your ovaries stop releasing eggs and producing reproductive hormones (primarily estrogen and progesterone). It's a normal part of aging, not a disease or medical condition, though it can cause uncomfortable symptoms that may benefit from treatment.
entries.definition: 12 consecutive months without a menstrual period
key_points: Caused by declining ovarian hormone production
Not a disease, but symptoms can be treated

entries.title: Average Age and Timeline
entries.content: The average age of menopause in the United States is 52 years old, but it's normal to reach menopause anywhere between ages 45-55. The transition to menopause (perimenopause) usually begins in your mid-40s and lasts an average of 4-8 years, though this varies widely. Some women transition quickly while others experience a longer perimenopause.

entries.title: Hormonal Changes
entries.description: What happens to hormones during menopause
entries.content: Menopause is driven by changes in reproductive hormones, primarily estrogen and progesterone. As you approach menopause, your ovaries gradually produce less of these hormones. During perimenopause, hormone levels fluctuate unpredictably - sometimes high, sometimes low - causing irregular periods and symptoms. After menopause, estrogen and progesterone remain at consistently low levels. These hormonal changes affect many body systems, causing the wide range of menopausal symptoms.
key_hormones: Estrogen: Declines significantly; affects many body systems
FSH (Follicle-Stimulating Hormone): Rises as ovaries produce less estrogen

entries.title: Natural vs. Induced Menopause
entries.content: Menopause can happen naturally as part of aging, or it can be induced by medical treatments or surgery. The symptoms and health implications are similar, but induced menopause often causes more sudden and severe symptoms because hormone levels drop abruptly rather than gradually.

types.description: Gradual decline in ovarian function with age; most common
types.characteristics: Gradual hormone decline, symptoms develop over years
Immediate menopause, often more severe symptoms due to sudden hormone drop

types.description: Caused by chemotherapy, radiation, or medications that affect ovaries
types.characteristics: Can be temporary or permanent; sudden onset

types.description: Ovaries stop functioning normally before age 40 without clear cause

entries.title: Impact on Daily Life
entries.description: How menopause affects quality of life and functioning
entries.content: Menopause can significantly impact daily life, relationships, work, and overall well-being. The severity of impact varies greatly - some women have minimal symptoms while others experience severe disruption. Common areas affected include sleep quality, work performance, relationships, sexual health, mental health, and social activities. It's important to know that effective treatments are available and you don't have to 'just suffer through it.'
areas_affected: Sleep: Disrupted by night sweats, insomnia
Work: Concentration problems, fatigue, hot flashes in meetings
Relationships: Mood changes, irritability, reduced libido
Sexual health: Vaginal dryness, pain, reduced desire
Mental health: Anxiety, depression, low self-esteem
Social life: Embarrassment about symptoms, social withdrawal
important_message: You don't have to suffer in silence
Seeking help is important for quality of life
Many women experience significant impact - you're not alone

entries.title: Who Experiences Menopause
entries.content: Menopause affects anyone who has ovaries and experiences menstrual periods. This includes cisgender women, transgender men who have not had ovaries removed, and non-binary individuals with ovaries. The experience and symptoms are the same regardless of gender identity. Everyone deserves access to information, support, and treatment for menopausal symptoms.
entries.who_it_affects: Anyone with ovaries who has had menstrual periods
entries.important_note: Gender identity doesn't change the biological process or symptoms; everyone deserves appropriate care

entries.title: Cardiovascular Health After Menopause
entries.description: Increased heart disease risk and prevention strategies
entries.content: Post-menopause cardiovascular risk significantly increases because dropping estrogen levels negatively impact cholesterol, blood pressure, and fat distribution. Estrogen has a protective effect on the heart, and its decline removes this protection. Heart disease becomes the leading cause of death for women after menopause, making heart-healthy habits crucial for prevention.
why_risk_increases: Estrogen's protective role: Estrogen helps regulate cholesterol and fat metabolism
Lipid profile changes: Higher LDL ('bad') cholesterol, lower HDL ('good') cholesterol, increased triglycerides
Small-dense LDL particles: More harmful particles that predict heart disease
Blood pressure: Often rises after menopause
Fat distribution: Shifts to abdominal fat, increasing heart risk
Metabolic changes: Increased risk of insulin resistance and diabetes
prevention_strategies: Regular exercise: 150 minutes/week of moderate activity (walking, cycling, dancing)
Healthy diet: Balanced nutrition, low sugar, controlled portions, Mediterranean-style diet
Don't smoke: Smoking significantly elevates cardiovascular risk
Manage weight: Maintain healthy weight through diet and exercise
Monitor health: Regular heart health screenings, blood pressure checks, cholesterol tests
Stress management: High stress worsens hormonal imbalances
Limit alcohol: Excessive alcohol increases blood pressure and heart risk
discuss_with_doctor: Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT): May lower heart disease risk if started within 10 years of menopause
Medications: For blood pressure or cholesterol if needed
Aspirin therapy: For some high-risk women
Regular screenings: ECG, stress tests if indicated

entries.title: Postmenopause Health Considerations
entries.description: Long-term health concerns and preventive care after menopause
entries.content: Postmenopause is the stage after reaching menopause, lasting for the rest of your life. While many menopausal symptoms ease up over time, postmenopausal women face increased risks for certain health conditions due to persistently low estrogen levels. Preventive care and healthy lifestyle choices are crucial for maintaining quality of life and longevity.
key_health_risks: Osteoporosis: Accelerated bone loss increases fracture risk
Cardiovascular disease: Leading cause of death in postmenopausal women
Genitourinary syndrome (GSM): Persistent vaginal and urinary symptoms without treatment
Type 2 diabetes: Increased risk due to metabolic changes
Cognitive changes: Some increased risk of dementia (research ongoing)
preventive_measures: Bone health: Calcium (1200mg/day), vitamin D (800 IU/day), weight-bearing exercise, DEXA scans
Heart health: Regular exercise, healthy diet, blood pressure and cholesterol monitoring
Vaginal health: Vaginal estrogen for persistent symptoms, regular sexual activity, moisturizers
Weight management: Balanced diet, regular exercise including strength training
Cancer screenings: Mammograms, cervical screening, colonoscopy as recommended
Mental health: Stay socially active, manage stress, seek help for depression/anxiety
hormone_therapy_considerations: Can continue HRT as long as benefits outweigh risks
Vaginal estrogen safe for long-term use
quality_of_life: Many symptoms improve 5-10 years after menopause
Some symptoms (vaginal dryness, urinary issues) may persist without treatment
Maintaining healthy lifestyle supports longevity and vitality
Women who start menopause after age 50 and have 40+ reproductive years may have increased longevity
when_to_see_doctor: Any post-menopausal bleeding (CRITICAL - see doctor immediately)
